title: Unveiling magmatic structures and connectivity beneath the lunar Oceanus Procellarum region from GRAIL gravity data

paper_content.abstract: The Oceanus Procellarum region, characterized by its vast basaltic plains and pronounced volcanic activity, serves as a focal point for understanding the volcanic history of the Moon. Here we present density models of the magmatic structures beneath Oceanus Procellarum, derived from Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory (GRAIL) mission data. The models uncover pronounced linear magmatic structures along the Procellarum’s western border and significant intrusions within the northern and southern Marius Hills. Crucially, they reveal three narrow near-horizontal sheeted magmatic conduits, 80-150 km long, extending from near-surface to 6-7 km depth. These magmatic conduits connect the Marius Hills’ northern and southern intrusions and bridge them with the Procellarum western border structures, suggesting that they likely served as central pathways facilitating magma transport across various volcanic systems. These discoveries reveal widespread magmatic connectivity beneath Oceanus Procellarum and underscore the critical role of lateral magma transport processes in shaping the Moon’s volcanic evolution.
paper_content.introduction:
Oceanus Procellarum, the largest mare on the Moon’s near side, is characterized by extensive basaltic plains and significant volcanic activity1. Uncovering its subsurface structures is pivotal for understanding lunar volcanism. Gravity data, which have played a crucial role in studying magma plumbing systems on rocky planets and satellites2–6, provide the ideal tool for such an investigation of Oceanus Procellarum. Forward modeling and inversion of gravity anomaly data enable the creation of density models of various magmatic structures that exhibit a density contrast with the surrounding rocks, such as shallow intrusions7–9, magmatic-related deposits10, and plutons11,12. Data from NASA’s Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory (GRAIL) mission have generated a high-resolution global map of the Moon’s gravity field. By modeling the gravity field to a spherical harmonic degree and order of 1200, a spatial resolution of 4.5 km by 4.5 km at the Moon’s equator was achieved13,14. Combined with topographic data from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA), these data aid the detection of small-scale features such as dykes7, ancient igneous intrusions3, buried impact craters15, and empty lava tubes16,17.

The volcanic legacy of the Oceanus Procellarum is exemplified by the Marius Hills volcanic complex (MHVC), a 35,000 km2 plateau, which exhibits the densest concentration of extrusive volcanic features on the Moon in the form of volcanic domes/shields and cones18,19. This region has consistently emerged as a prominent site for lunar exploration, primarily due to its distinctive geological characteristics and the valuable insights it offers into lunar volcanism20–23. Utilizing gravity data from the Lunar Prospector spacecraft24 and the GRAIL mission25,26, two quasi-circular, positive gravity anomalies within the MHVC (north and south) were identified and modeled as two massive sill/dyke groups that are responsible for the volcanic activity in this region. Investigation into the surface distribution of volcanic vents confirms the presence of the zones of magma accumulation27. However, magmatic structures beneath the MHVC and surrounding areas and processes by which magma is transported to the shallow crustal depths remain enigmatic to date28,29.

GRAIL gravity data revealed a pattern of narrow linear anomalies that border the Procellarum KREEP Terrane (PKT)5. The source of anomalies is interpreted to be solidified lava within rifts and the feeder dykes beneath them, which likely served as the magma plumbing system for much of the nearside mare volcanism. The MHVC is positioned roughly 200 km east of the PKT’s western border structures. Previous research has primarily examined these volcanic systems independently5,24–27,30, overlooking the critical magmatic structures between them and their collective impact on volcanism in the Oceanus Procellarum. This oversight underscores a significant gap in our understanding of the magmatic architecture beneath the MHVC and the PKT’s western border, highlighting the importance of considering these systems as interconnected entities to comprehend the extensive volcanic activity fully in the Oceanus Procellarum region.

In this work, to better understand the magmatic architecture beneath the Oceanus Procellarum, we apply a three-dimensional (3D) inversion technique to the GRAIL gravity data to construct detailed 3D density models. The magmatic structures, characterized by higher density than the host rocks, can be recovered through the inversion of the Bouguer gravity anomaly, which plays a key role in understanding the magmatic sources and processes2,7,9,31. This study encompasses the southern and northern MHVC, the western border structures of the PKT, and their neighboring areas, enabling a comprehensive understanding of their interconnections, and facilitating their integration into the wider PKT region. The detailed modeling of these magmatic structures provides valuable information regarding the formation of volcanic landforms, magma transport, and energy exchange across various lunar systems.
paper_content.results:
Bouguer gravity data and topography
Figure 1a shows the topography of the lunar near side derived from the MoonTopo2600p model based on data collected by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter mission32. GRAIL gravity data extracted from the GRGM1200B model13 were used for this study. The Bouguer gravity anomaly (Fig. 1b) used for imaging the subsurface structures was derived from SHTools33 with a reference radius of 1738 km. To remove the gravitational contribution of the surface topography, a crust density of 2800 kg/m3 was used for Bouguer correction34. To eliminate long-wavelength variations in the crustal structure and short-wavelength noise, we filtered the Bouguer gravity data to include data between degree and order 7 and degree and order 660, yielding a half-wavelength surface resolution of ~8 km. A cosine taper was implemented between degrees 550 and 660 to reduce high-frequency ringing35.

Study area A (Fig. 1) covers the MHVC and partial western border structures of the PKT5. The Bouguer gravity anomaly (Figs. 1b and 2b) reveals two quasi-circular mass anomalies, marked as Marius-NH (northern half) and Marius-SH (southern half) based on their locations relative to the Marius crater26. The two anomalies exhibit maximum amplitudes of 165 and 169 mGal, respectively. Marius Hills plateau, corresponding to the northern anomaly, contains most domes and cones situated in a localized highland. In contrast, the southern anomaly covers fewer volcanic domes without elevated topography. A narrow linear positive gravity anomaly, ranging from ~40 to ~70 mGal, connects these two quasi-circular anomalies, forming a “bridge” that has been identified in an earlier study24. Furthermore, a significant high-gravity anomaly belt, spanning ~800 km with a NNW–SSE orientation and peaking at 183 mGal, is identified. This belt has been interpreted to be part of the magmatic border structures of the PKT region5. The linear gravity anomaly extends NNW and diverges into three thinner branches at the northwestern border of the PKT (Figs. 1b and 3b). Study area B (Figs. 1 and 3a, b) includes the western and middle branches of the northwestern border, each marked by distinct linear gravity anomalies with a general NNW–SSE orientation, spanning over 500 km and displaying values from ~30 to 138 mGal. The western edges of the belt gravity anomalies (Figs. 2b and 3b) are generally coincident with steep topographic gradients leading up to the adjacent highlands (Figs. 2a and 3a), while their eastern sides show less topographical correlation. Prominent wrinkle ridges (Supplementary Fig. 1) run parallel to the belt gravity anomaly in study area A and the belt gravity anomalies of the middle and eastern branches in study area B, exhibiting a NNW–SSE orientation. Also, a distinct set of wrinkle ridges (Supplementary Fig. 1) traversing the Marius Hills region predominantly adheres to this NNW–SSE trend36.

3D inversion density models from Bouguer gravity data
The 3D inversion technique applied here is based on the probabilistic method37 to generate 3D density models by inverting gravity data. The method was assessed and proven successful in identifying the density structures of both the upper and lower crust of the Earth9,38–44. A significant advantage of this inversion approach is its capacity to integrate a priori information regarding physical properties, spatial extent, depth, and orientation of the source bodies via the covariance matrix to construct an accurate and reliable solution. To address the non-uniqueness inherent in the inversion process, we performed a sensitivity analysis on several critical parameters that could affect the inversion results, including the covariance matrix parameter, the depth weighting function, and the depth extent of the inversion domain (see “Methods” section for more details).

Figures 2c–e and 3c–e display the 3D density models for the two study areas, which represent optimal models obtained from inversions using the best-fitting parameters (see “Methods” section for more details). The 3D density models recovered from the Bouguer gravity data with a half-wavelength surface resolution of ~8 km facilitate the investigation of complex subsurface magmatic structures in detail. Given the geological evidence for potential intrusive activity24,25,27, the 3D continuous density inversions are volume-rendered using discrete cutoffs to delineate the extent of possible intrusive bodies. The red surfaces indicate the density contrast iso-surface of 160 kg/m3, which outlines high-density bodies that we interpret as magmatic bodies. The yellow surfaces depict a higher density contrast iso-surface of 350 kg/m3 to delineate even denser magmatic bodies. The top depth corresponds to either the shallowest limit of the magmatic bodies or the deepest extent of impact brecciation, where the density contrast fades. The bottom depth denotes the base of the magmatic bodies or where the density contrast with surrounding rocks significantly diminishes.

Figures 4 and 5 show horizontal and vertical cross-sections through the inverted density models for the two study areas. The blue dashed lines indicate the 160 kg/m3 density contrast contour lines. The assumed density contrast iso-surface of 160 kg/m3 for the magmatic body does not consider potential density changes amongst the magmatic rocks, and could over- or underestimate the size and depth of the magmatic bodies and thus presents a limitation and potential source of error in interpretation. When using the iso-surfaces of 150 and 170 kg/m3 as the interpreted magmatic bodies, the total volume increases by 5% and decreases by 6%, respectively, compared to the 160 kg/m3 iso-surfaces.

Figures 2c, 3c, 4, and 5 exhibit distinct belt structures oriented NNW–SSE with density contrasts ranging from 160 to ~700 kg/m3. These belt structures correspond to the belt gravity anomalies depicted in Figs. 2b and 3b and match the PKT border magmatic intrusions as identified in a previous study5. We observe that the density contrast of the intrusions from the inversion gradually decreases from the center to the edges. This is mainly due to the smoothing nature of the inversion method used44; the actual density contrast variation within the intrusions may not be as pronounced. The density model for area A (Figs. 2c and 4) shows that the border intrusion spans from near the surface down to depths of 10–13 km with a length of ~800 km, a thickness of 8–11 km, and a width of 130–270 km. In study area B, the western branch intrusion is ~600 km in length, ~140 km in width, and ~8–10 km in thickness, and the middle branch intrusion is about 550 km long, 80 km wide, with a thickness ranging from 5 to 9 km. The western PKT border intrusions become thinner and narrower, and the depth of the top surface increases toward the north.

The inversion density model indicates that the Marius-NH intrusion (Figs. 2d and 4f, h) and Marius-SH intrusion (Figs. 2e and 4e, h), reported in the literature24,25, extend down to depths of 11 and 12 km, with thicknesses of 10.2 and 9.7 km, respectively. The Marius-NH body spans ~100 km in diameter, while the Marius-SH body spans ~130 km. The density contrasts of these two intrusions lie between 160 and 720 kg/m3, with the maximum value in the upper center of the intrusions. Both intrusions have a bowl-like shape. Moreover, a significant magmatic body (located at 55.7°W, 12.9°N; see Figs. 2c, d and 4a, b, f) characterized by a quasi-circular configuration is located adjacent to the west of the Marius-NH intrusion. This body has a diameter of ~90 km, a thickness of ~6 km, and is positioned beneath the more subdued western inclines of the elevated Marius Hills plateau. A magmatic body (located at 55.3°W, 6.3°N; see Figs. 2c, e and 4a, b, e) of similar dimensions, with a diameter of ~80 km and a thickness of ~5 km, is identified. The intrusion is located directly beneath the Reiner crater at a shallow depth (3.5 km; Fig. 4a) and tilts slightly southwestward at a deeper depth (5.5 km; Fig. 4b). Both of these two magmatic bodies were neither discovered nor mentioned in previous studies15,24–26.

It is noteworthy that the inversion density model for study area A (Figs. 2c and 4) reveals a complex network of connectivity among the various volcanic systems under investigation. The Marius-NH and Marius-SH intrusions are interconnected with a narrow corridor of dense rocks extending ~80 km in length, 50 km in width, and 5 km in thickness (Figs. 2c and 4a, b, h). The narrow corridor is sill-like in structure and nearly horizontal. Furthermore, another two sill-like narrow corridors connect the two intrusions with the western border structures. The southern magmatic conduit, which traverses the intrusion beneath the Reiner crater, is ~130 km long, 50 km wide, and 5 km thick (Figs. 2c and 4a, b, e). The northern magmatic conduit, crossing the quasi-circular intrusion adjacent to the west side of the Marius-NH intrusion, measures ~110 km in length, 55 km in width, and 6 km in thickness (Figs. 2c and 4a, b, f).

A lower density of 2560 kg/m3 and a higher density of 3000 kg/m3 were also used for Bouguer corrections to derive the Bouguer anomalies, which were then inverted to construct density models, as detailed in Supplementary Fig. 2. The impact of conducting the Bouguer correction using different density values on the resultant Bouguer gravity anomaly is especially pronounced in regions with significant terrain variations, such as the Reiner crater (Supplementary Fig. 3a) and Marius-NH (Supplementary Fig. 4a). The higher density of 3000 kg/m3 yields the best-fit Bouguer correction for the craters (Supplementary Fig. 3a), which is similar to the mean density estimated for the mare45 (~3090 kg/m3) and the bulk density estimated for the Marius Hills surface basalts (3150 kg/m3) based on observations from the Lunar Prospector Gamma Ray Spectrometer46,47. However, it also significantly enhances the western belt gravity anomalies (Supplementary Fig. 3a) due to the relatively low topography in that area. Ultimately, we opted for a density of 2800 kg/m3 as a more representative choice for the entire region. The comparison of inversion models (Supplementary Fig. 2) shows that as the Bouguer correction density is increased, there is a slight increase in the volume of the western PKT border intrusion in study area A and the western branch in study area B. Conversely, the volumes of the middle branch intrusion in study area B, the Marius-NH intrusion, and the sill-like narrow corridors identified above decrease slightly. However, these effects are limited, and the main structural characteristics of the high-density bodies in this region exhibit highly consistent geometries.

To minimize the potential influence of crustal thinning on the inversion models, which is characterized by relatively long-wavelength positive gravity signals, we filtered signals with wavelengths <11 degrees (Supplementary Fig. 5a, c), and a subsequent 3D inversion was performed. The inversion results (Supplementary Fig. 5b, d) indicate a modest reduction in the lateral spread of the PKT border structures and a 2–3 km shallowing of their bases. These two inversion models may more accurately reflect the border structures by removing the effect of crustal thinning. Nevertheless, we observed reduction in both the volume and maximum density contrast of the intrusions beneath Marius-SH and Marius-NH as well as the sill-like narrow corridors (Supplementary Figs. 3e, 4e, and 5b), where mantle uplift is deemed improbable24,25,48,49. Moreover, the middle branch structures of the northwestern border become discontinuous (Supplementary Fig. 5d). Thus, it seems that filtering out gravity signals lower than degree and order 11 has simultaneously affected the long-wavelength signals associated with shallow sources.

Beyond study areas A and B, we also examined the Flamsteed region (labeled as C in Supplementary Fig. 1) and the Aristarchus plateau region (labeled as D in Supplementary Fig. 1) within the Oceanus Procellarum. These features were also analyzed, though the interpretation of magmatic structures remains uncertain. However, neither the southern Aristarchus plateau nor the Flamsteed region appears to connect with the western PKT border intrusions. As a consequence, our discussion is focused on the inversion models (Figs. 2–5) in study areas A and B, which are derived from the Bouguer gravity data spanning from degree and order 7 to degree and order 660, following Bouguer correction with a crust density of 2800 kg/m3.
paper_content.methods:
The 3D inversion technique used in this research leverages a probabilistic method to generate 3D density models from gravity data37, which has been shown to be effective in identifying crustal structures on Earth9,38,39,94. The objective function employed for the inversion of gravity data is as follows:

\Phi = (G m - d_{obs})^T C_D^{-1} (G m - d_{obs}) + (m - m_{apr})^T C_M^{-1} (m - m_{apr}) (1)

Here, m represents the model parameter vector, values of the densities of the cells, d_{obs} is the gravity data vector, and G is the forward modeling matrix where Gm = d. The first term of Eq. (1) signifies the data misfit function, weighted by the data error covariance matrix, C_D. The second term corresponds to the stabilizing function, which accounts for the deviation of model parameters m from a reference model m_{apr}, weighted by the model covariance matrix, C_M.

The a priori information, including physical properties, spatial extent, depth, and orientation of the source bodies, can be incorporated via C_M to constrain the inversion and achieve an accurate and reliable solution.

To minimize the objective function, the solution is derived below37

m_e = m_{apr} + C_M G^T (G C_M G^T + C_D)^{-1} (d_{obs} - G m_{apr}) (2)

To counteract the natural decay of the forward modeling matrix with increasing depth, a depth weight function with the following form was used:

w(z) = 1 / (z_{max} - z)^\beta (3)

where z_{max} is the maximum depth of the inversion domain and z is the depth of each cell. \beta is the exponent of the depth weight function and \beta = 1 was used for this study.

The solution with the depth weighting function is:

m_e = m_{apr} + W^{-1} C_M W^{-1} G^T (G W^{-1} C_M W^{-1} G^T + C_D)^{-1} (d_{obs} - G m_{apr}) (4)

The parameters of the model covariance matrix C_M for areas A and B are listed in Table 1. We utilized a nested covariance model, as detailed in the second and third rows of Table 1, since the Bouguer gravity anomaly (Figs. 2b and 3b) within this region displays characteristics that span multiple scales. Specifically, the border structures of the PKT present larger linear formations trending NNW, while anomalies like the Marius-SH and Marius-NH appear to be relatively smaller quasi-circular in nature. Data error covariance matrix C_D is a diagonal matrix where each diagonal element is set at 2 mGal, representing an approximate estimate of the noise level in the Bouguer gravity data. A zero-reference model (m_{apr} = 0) was used for the inversions.

Before conducting the inversion, the Bouguer gravity data were transformed from spherical to Cartesian coordinates. The inversion domain was divided into numerous prism cells with dimensions of 1.5 km \times 1.5 km \times 0.25 km in the x, y, and depth directions, respectively. The depth extent of the inversion domain was set at 20 km. To mitigate edge effects during the inversion, the spatial dimensions of the inversion domain were expanded by 30 km in all lateral directions beyond the data coverage. This parameterization results in a model with 534 \times 526 \times 80 cells in study area A, 433 \times 467 \times 80 cells in study area B. The top of the inversion domain was constrained by the topographic data. Therefore, the cells above the terrain were removed and not inverted. By constraining the top of the terrain, it is possible to mitigate the effects caused by inaccurate terrain-corrected densities and fully take into account the rapid changes in depth within the craters, thereby improving the accuracy of the inversion model. We observed positive topographic elevations in specific localized sections, mainly the rims of large craters located in the lower left corners of areas A (Fig. 2a) and B (Fig. 3a). During the inversion process, the topographic elevations of these regions were set to zero, as their very limited area did not impact our inversion results.

Supplementary Fig. 9a, b shows the difference maps between the observed gravity anomalies (Figs. 2a and 3a) and the predicted gravity anomalies calculated from the 3D inversion models (Figs. 4 and 5). The difference maps show how well the inverted models resemble the observed gravity. The standard deviations of the differences for study areas A (Supplementary Fig. 9a) and B (Supplementary Fig. 9b) are 1.3 and 1.2 mGal, respectively, with a mean of 0.0 mGal. In Supplementary Fig. 9a, we observe short-wavelength fluctuations appearing as narrow strips, with widths of 6–10 km and lengths spanning 20–100 km, exhibiting a distinct S-N orientation. The short-wavelength jitters presented in Supplementary Fig. 9 black a clear directional pattern. The short-wavelength jitters are mainly related to the orbit-parallel striping in the GRAIL data at high degree17. These fluctuations are not anticipated to disrupt the primary magmatic structures in this study, as the latter possess scales significantly larger than those of the strips.

The inversion method introduced above was proposed in the Cartesian coordinate system and can be directly extended to the spherical coordinate system. However, the inversion process can be much more efficient in the Cartesian coordinate system, where the inversion space can be divided into a series of adjacent prisms of the same size, and the FFT technique can highly speed up the inversion process94. To investigate the effect of the lunar curvature for this study, we inverted the Bouguer gravity in study areas A and B in the spherical coordinate system separately (Supplementary Fig. 10a, b). The resulting density models show a high degree of similarity to the models obtained in the Cartesian coordinate system (Figs. 2c and 3c) in terms of the density contrasts and the spatial extent of the inverted anomalies. However, due to the utilization of finer cells (1.5 km \times 1.5 km \times 0.25 km), the model in the Cartesian coordinate system reveals more detailed structures than in the spherical coordinate system (0.15° \times 0.15° \times 0.25 km), in which the cell size was limited by computational performance. Therefore, this study presents and discusses the inversion results using the Cartesian coordinate system.

Several factors can influence inversion results when using the probabilistic method described above, including the parameters of the model covariance matrix (C_M), the depth weighting function, and the depth extent of the inversion domain. To assess the impact of these factors, we conducted a sensitivity analysis and compared the inversion results obtained with varying parameter settings (refer to the Supplementary for details; Supplementary Figs. 11, 12, and 13). These factors primarily have a modest impact on the thicknesses of the high-density bodies. The connectivity between the western PKT border intrusion and the northern and southern intrusions remains distinctly apparent. After comparing the inversion density models with previous studies on the northern and southern intrusions of the Marius Hills24,25 and the middle branch intrusion5 in study area B, through forward modeling, we selected the optimal models for study areas A and B shown in Figs. 2 and 3, as they demonstrate better agreement with these earlier studies. These models are derived using a \beta value of 1, an inversion domain depth extent of 20 km, and the model covariance parameters are listed in Table 1.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors have combined gravity and topography data to explore the subsurface density structure of a major volcanic province on the Moon in an attempt to throw light on the volcanic plumbing system. Extremely interesting results are obtained that support and significantly expand on previousy-published ideas about the sub-surface volcanic systems in the areas studied.
I am not an expert on the mathematical techniques used in the analysis. However, I am happy to comment on the authors' geophysical interpretation of their results, and find these to be entirely plausible.
I have line-numbered a copy of the Word file of the text and linked the following questions and minor editorial suggestions to it.
line 20. I suggest you remove the "'s" from the end of "Procellarum's".
line 81. Why did you select the specific value 2,800 kg/m3 for the higher crustal density used to derive the Bouguer anomaly? And looking at Fig. 6a, how does the presence of the surface volcanics, presumably significantly denser than the anorthosite crust unless they were very vesicular, influence this part of the analysis?
line 128. The word "which" makes no sense here and should be deleted.
lines 131-140. The shortest dimension of the bodies in Area B is 5 to 7.5 km. Have you given any thought to the likely survival time against conductive cooling of magma bodies with these dimensions? A calculation based on
(distance of travel of thermal wave) = ~2 x SQRT(thermal diffusivity x time)
would suggest that with a thermal diffusivity of say 5 times 10 to the power -7 meters-squared per second, a 5 km thick body
would cool significantly in ~400 thousand years.
line 140. It is better to change "as the range goes" to "toward the".
line 168. Use "less than" rather than "under".
line 257. I suggest you add "horizontal" after "long" for clarity.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript presents analyses of gravity data for the Marius Hills region of the Moon, one of the few large volcanic constructs on the Moon that is an area of high interest. Previous work found evidence for large intrusive bodies below the Marius Hills. Separately, a previous study identified a large set of linear gravity anomalies surrounding the nearside
Procellarum KREEP terrane interpreted as the magma plumbing system of the nearside maria. This study makes the case
that the intrusions below the Marius hills are connected to the linear anomalies in the region as part of a more complex and
integrated magma system related to the magma plumbing of the maria and Marius hills.
Overall, I find this to be a very interesting and well-written manuscript. This is a novel and potentially important interpretation
that is well supported by the manuscript. Overall, I find the connection between the Marius Hills volcanism and the PKT
border structures to be an interesting and important result. This connection clearly has important implications for the volcanic
evolution of the Moon. However, the manuscript could do better in laying out exactly what the broader implications of this
new interpretation are. How does this new interpretation change our overall understanding of lunar volcanism?
Below I include a number of line-by-line comments for the authors to consider
[82-86] I am glad to see you tested two density values for the Bouguer correction. Since your region of interest is within the
maria, a higher density would be appropriate (~3000 kg/m3; see Goossens 2022). This choice could have a noticeable
impact for your analysis of the Marius Hills themselves, which appear dominantly basaltic and do have considerable relief.
This is particularly true for the Marius NH anomaly, in which your Bouguer map shows a positive Bouguer anomaly beneath
an area of positive topography - using an overly low density in the Bouguer correction contributes to this positive Bouguer
anomaly. Given the relief of 2-3 km, a Bouguer correction density of 2500 rather than 3000 would contribute an extra 40-60
mGal, which is not trivial in comparison to the observed value of 150 mGal in your Bouguer map. I would recommend
focusing on the higher density value that you tested (2800 rather than 2550).
[90] It would be best not to justify the choice of density based on the density of feldspathic rocks given your study site in the
maria.
[Figure 2] This is a matter of personal preference, but I find these sorts of perspective views draped on topography to
obscure rather than reveal information. There is no new information in the topographic drape that is not also in a flat simple
color map. The perspective adds distortion (including areas in which the data cannot be seen behind a topographic high).
Simple map views as in Figure 4 are preferable. The perspective views of the isosurfaces in Figure 3 are a useful way to
supplement a simple map view (though figure 2c is in a different perspective than 2b, causing some confusion).
[120] Please include a brief description of the methodology in the main text, which can refer to the supplement for more
detail. Please also include a brief statement/discussion of non-uniqueness in the main text, with more detail in the appendix.
Inversions of gravity data like this are fundamentally non-unique - this is not a weakness of this study which is using an
accepted and rigorous approach for inverting the gravity data, but it should be acknowledged. This data could also be (and
has also been) inverted assuming that these same gravity anomalies arise from thickness variations in the maria, or
variations in dense layers below the crust. 3D inversions are particularly non-unique and rely on added assumptions and
constraints, and this requires more discussion in the manuscript and supplement. The inversions and interpretations in this
study are sound and are very interesting, but some discussion of this non-uniqueness and alternative interpretations is
needed. It would also be good to include geological evidence supporting the inversions - for example, given the surface
volcanism associated with the marius hills and the strong anomalies that have been previously interpreted as sill-like
intrusions, the interpretation of the other linear anomalies as large intrusive bodies is geologically reasonable.
[147] “The densities of these intrusions lie between…” This statement depends on the density of the surrounding medium. At
these depth ranges, these intrusions are presumably surrounded by feldspathic crust (unlike the basaltic surface material,
see above), thus the lower density surrounding medium is reasonable. The reduction in porosity at depth may have an effect
also. Some discussion of these matters (perhaps in the supplement) is warranted.
[145] “reported in the literature” Added discussion of how these inversion results compare with the previous simpler study
would help.
[149] Please give the coordinates of the centers of these newly discovered features. Could these two “bowl-like” features
actually be impact craters that were filled in by the mare volcanism (e.g., ref 15)?
[152-155] The intrusion inferred beneath Reiner crater is interesting, but I have some concerns. In the Bouguer maps, it does
not appear that there is a positive Bouguer anomaly centered on the crater. Because of the different perspective view for the
density model, it is difficult to see how the density anomaly interpreted as an intrusion compares to the crater. This is also an
area where the Bouguer correction density matters - using too low of a density for the Bouguer correction will result in a relict
negative gravity anomaly over the crater itself (this can be seen in figure 2b), which will affect the inversion (though cannot
explain the positive density anomaly discussed here).
[167] “To minimize the potential influence of crustal thinning…” I appreciate the inclusion of this section. In practice, any
gravity anomalies below about degree 80 can be ascribed to crustal thickness variations, though they may also be explained
by intrusive bodies. Some added discussion of this non-uniqueness and the merits of the different interpretations would be
helpful.
[255-257] “However, the origin of the magmatic conduits, their role in the regional magmatic transport, and their impacton the
volcanic evolution in the Procellarum Oceanus region demand further inquiry.” This is a very important point, and the lack of
a more substantive discussion of this point is a shortcoming of this manuscript. The manuscript shows that the Marius Hills
may be connected to larger regional elongated anomalies that may represent the magma plumbing of the region - but what
does it all mean? Previous studies interpreted the linear anomalies as related to the magma plumbing system of this region,
and interpreted the Marius Hills gravity as related to subsurface intrusions. How does this new study connecting the two
change our understanding of the evolution of this region and the Moon? The manuscript could go further in addressing the
broader significance.
[264-265] This discussion of vertical dikes vs lateral sills raises a question - previous work interpreted the linear structures
as related to dike-like structures based on their linearity. In the new interpretation in this study, why are the elongated gravity
anomalies that connect the MH anomalies to each other and to the PKT border structures linear? The gravity inversions are
consistent with sill-like intrusions, but those sill like intrusions are greatly elongated in one direction.
[370] The methods describe a depth weighting as is commonly invoked in these types of models. Is wz the only component
of the overall weighting matrix W? Other models have also included model smoothness criteria, and used a regularized
inversion - is this also done in this model?
[374-375] The choice of different values of beta (exponent in the depth weighting) for the two study areas seems odd. Please
show inversions for both values of beta for both areas and provide more discussion in the supplement.
Some of the references are incomplete, giving only authors, title, and year without journal information.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This study makes use of GRAIL data to investigate the subsurface magmatic structures of two regions within the Oceanus
Procellarum: (1) Procellarum’s western border and (2) Northern and Southern Marius Hills. To achieve this objective, 3D
inversion technique is employed to translate the GRAIL gravity data and construct detailed 3D density models of the
subsurface to understand the density distribution beneath the specified regions. Examining the 3D density models, authors
suggest an interconnected sill-like magmatic conduits’ network beneath the Oceanus Procellarum connecting the northern
and southern halves of the Marius Hills as well as the border structures of the Procellarum region. The proposal of a ‘bridge’
between the northern and southern halves of the Marius Hills was proposed by Kiefer (2013). This research, for the first time,
provides evidence for the connected subsurface structures not only for the MHVC but also for the adjacent regions.
Further, this finding of interlinked subsurface magmatic structures is also suggested to be accountable for the existing ages
and compositional differences between the older domes of the MHVC and the younger mare flows in the region. This paper
proposes that the younger mare flows of the MHVC could have been originated from the deep feeder dykes beneath the
western border of the Procellarum terrain as these regions exhibit a connected subsurface magmatic structure in the derived
3D density models.
Two previously undiscovered magmatic intrusions situated west of the northern Marius intrusion and to the southwest of the
Reiner crater have also been detected for the very first time from the derived density models of this paper. These newly
identified magmatic bodies are inferred to serve as potential filled and buried impact craters.
Overall, this study and observations are good as they play a crucial role in understanding the magma plumbing system and
their subsurface behaviour as the norm. It highlights the importance of looking at the regional geological context while
examining magmatism in a region on the Moon. However, the arguments presented in the study needs to be substantiated
by the compositional and temporal relationships to build a complete picture of volcanism in the Oceanus Procellarum. In
this view, ‘Major revisions’ are suggested in the manuscript. I suggest the following comments be incorporated within the
manuscript:
(1) The title of the manuscript implies that the magmatic structures and interconnections existing in the entire Oceanus
Procellarum have been examined, which would have been a very significant contribution. However, the study emphasizes
primarily on the MHVC of the Oceanus Procellarum. Examination of the surrounding regions of Aristarchus, Flamsteed etc.
is suggested to observe if such interconnections also exist in these areas.
(2) The Results and Discussion section needs reorganization having separate section on ‘Study Area A’ and ‘Study Area B’
for clarity and emphasis on the importance of both these regions. Further, the importance of the ‘Study Area B’ needs to be
discussed in detail.
(3) Carry out a detailed mineralogical analysis of the region. This is essential to substantiate the proposed hypothesis of
interconnections, as shown in Fig. 6. The smaller craters in the area may provide important insights regarding the same.
(4) The temporal relationships between the formation of the domes, surrounding basalts and the wrinkle ridges need to be
discussed.
Additionally, the following concerns are needed to be addressed:
(1) Authors are suggesting that the magma that accumulates beneath the craters need not to have deep crustal or mantle
origin. Rather, they can migrate through the fractures present in the lunar crust. To make such a statement, it is necessary to
address the factors that control the magma transport at shallow crustal levels and the local structural features that exert
control over the magma migration.
(2) Line 132, What is the level of uncertainties or errors?
(3) Line 194, It is not clear from the description that how it can be inferred from the 3D inversion model that initially 3 discrete
magma chambers gradually interconnected with the progress in the filling processes. This needs to be elaborated.
(4) Line 222-224, In order to establish that the buried magma intrusion in the region exerted structural controls on the wrinkle
ridges, it is important to constrain to timescale of these two processes. In case of a younger magmatic episode, it is also
possible that the wrinkle ridges controlled the emplacement of the magmatic unit. Consider this, especially since this region
has experienced prolonged magmatic activity.
(5) Lines 266-272, Is megaregolith the only cause for the formation of the interconnections? Do subsurface structural
features such as faults associated with the wrinkle ridges have a role to play?
(6) Lines 272-273 It is mentioned that higher heat flux in the PKT region could have played a role in these magmatic
activities. How?
(7) Line 322, Deep feeder dykes below the PKT border are not shown in the schematic fig. 6.
(8) Line 323-325. It is essential to discuss the implications of the proposed scenario on the mineralogy and the surface age
of the basalts in the region to substantiate the findings. I suggest a brief discussion on the same may be provided.
(9) Line 333, “100nT” looks typo error; instead, it should be “100mGal”
(10) The paper is generally well-written, presenting some interesting and significant results, but the novelty of the study
needs to be brought out and highlighted more clearly and prominently.

Comments: The authors have combined gravity and topography data to explore the subsurface

s of the
surface volcanics, presumably significantly denser than the anorthosite crust unless they were very

Comments: lines 131-140. The shortest dimension of the bodies in Area B is 5 to 7.5 km. Have

thousand years.
Response: Thank you very much for providing the idea of estimating cooling time for magma
bodies. This could make for a fascinating study, especially in the context of the Moon's
Procellarum KREEP Terrane (PKT). The simple model used here assumes that cooling occurs
solely through thermal conduction, disregarding other heat transfer mechanisms such as
convection and radiation. To make a more reasonable estimation of the cooling time of magma
bodies, other factors like the initial temperature of the magma, ambient temperature, size and shape
of the magma body, magma composition, crystallization during cooling, and pressure conditions
need to be considered. PKT is a geochemically distinct region on the Moon, characterized by a
thin lunar crust and a high concentration of radiogenic heat-producing elements that are considered
to have driven the thermal evolution of the lunar mantle in this region. How these factors affect
magma evolution and cooling in the PKT region needs careful simulation. Therefore, using this
simple model to estimate cooling times presents many challenges. For these reasons, we did not
discuss the survival time of the magmatic bodies. However, our 3D magmatic modelswill provide

important consideration in future research efforts.

surrounded by feldspathic crust (unlike the basaltic surface material, see above), thus the lower

Response: Thank you for your insightful comments. We agree that the density of the surrounding

intrusions. Therefore, more factors needed to be considered and discussed when using absolute
density to interpret the magmatic bodies. In the revised manuscript, we used density contrast
instead of absolute density to show and interpret magmatic intrusions. This will simplify the
density interpretation. This is also consistent with the way magmatic bodies have been interpreted

Comments: [145] “reported in the literature” Added discussion of how these inversion results

Response: Thank you for your comments. These inversion results were carefully compared with
the previous simpler study in the Discussion (refer to Lines 238-251).
Comments: [149] Please give the coordinates of the centers of these newly discovered features.
Could these two “bowl-like” features actually be impact craters that were filled in by the mare
volcanism (e.g., ref 15)?
Response: Thank you for your suggestion. We added the coordinates for the three inferred buried
craters identified from our inversion models.
Evans et al. (2016) (ref. 15) analyzed GRAIL Bouguer gravity anomalies and proposed that the
circular features at Marius Hills may be buried impact craters, caused by the density contrast
between the feldspathic crust and mare basalt infill. Zhang et al. (2018) suggested that volcanic
features in the area could be intruded sills beneath craters and concluded that impact craters may
create crustal weaknesses favorable for sill and dike intrusions. Our inversion models are
consistent with these findings. Besides the two “bowl-like” features in Marius Hills, intrusions
with various volumes have been discovered beneath many craters, including but not limited to the
inferred filled and buried crater adjacent to the Marius-NH (Fig. 2d), Reiner crater (Fig. 2e),
Marius crater (Fig. 2d), Briggs B crater (Fig. 3d), Lichtenberg crater (Fig. 3d), Seleucus crater (Fig.

Comments: [152-155] The intrusion inferred beneath Reiner crater is interesting, but I have some

area where the Bouguer correction density matters - using too low of a density for the Bouguer
correction will result in a relict negative gravity anomaly over the crater itself (this can be seen in

compared the Bouguer gravity anomalies across the Reiner crater using different crust densities

best-fit Bouguer correction for the Reiner crater (Supplementary Fig. 3a), which is similar to the
mean density estimated for the mare (Neumann et al., 2018) (~3090 kg/m³) and the bulk density
estimated for the Marius Hills surface basalts (3150 kg/m3) based on observations from the Lunar
Prospector Gamma Ray Spectrometer (Kiefer et al., 2012; Prettyman et al., 2006). However, it
also significantly enhances the western belt gravity anomalies (Supplementary Fig. 3a) due to the
relatively low topography in that area. Ultimately, we opted for a density of 2,800 kg/m³ as a more
representative choice for the entire region.
It appears that with the increasing Bouguer gravity amplitude over the Reiner crater, it, along with
the surrounding gravity anomaly signals, form longer-wavelength gravity signals (see
Supplementary Fig. 3a). Consequently, the inverted density model shows an increase in the density
contrast at depth while the density contrast of the magmatic intrusion beneath the Reiner crater
decreases slightly (see Supplementary Figs. 3b-3d). However, the connectivity between the PKT
border structures and the Marius-SH remains unchanged.
In the density horizontal slice maps (Fig. 4a-4c), we added black circles to indicate the location of
the Reiner crater and Marius crater so that the spatial relationship between craters and intrusions
can be observed more clearly. As can be seen from Fig. 4, the intrusion is located directly beneath
the Reiner crater at a shallow depth (3.5 km; see Fig. 4a) and slightly tilts southwestward with
increasing depth (5.5 km; see Fig. 4b).

the inversion process, we performed a sensitivity analysis on several critical parameters that could
affect the inversion results, including the covariance matrix parameter, the depth weighting
function, and the depth extent of the inversion domain (see Method for more details). The inversion
models underwent slight modifications with changes in the settings, particularly affecting the
density distribution in the depth direction due to the low resolution of the gravity data. This resulted
in alterations to the size of the magmatic intrusions and the values of density contrast. This reflects
the inherent non-uniqueness of gravity data inversion, where anomalous bodies of different sizes
and densities can produce the same gravity anomalies. However, as evident, the main structures of
the magmatic bodies remain consistent with one another. Moreover, the model of crustal thickness
variations was discussed in Lines 275-280. Given the potential magma chamber compartments
revealed by the 3D inversion model, as well as intrusions identified beneath the Marius Hills that
could have contributed to facilitating surface volcanism, the interpretation of linear anomalies as
large intrusions appears to be geologically reasonable.
Comments: [255-257] “However, the origin of the magmatic conduits, their role in the regional
magmatic transport, and their impact on the volcanic evolution in the Procellarum Oceanus region
demand further inquiry.” This is a very important point, and the lack of a more substantive
discussion of this point is a shortcoming of this manuscript. The manuscript shows that the Marius
Hills may be connected to larger regional elongated anomalies that may represent the magma
plumbing of the region - but what does it all mean? Previous studies interpreted the linear
anomalies as related to the magma plumbing system of this region, and interpreted the Marius
Hills gravity as related to subsurface intrusions. How does this new study connecting the two
change our understanding of the evolution of this region and the Moon? The manuscript could go
further in addressing the broader significance.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comments and suggestions. The discussion primarily
focuses on these issues. We have revised the article to make our arguments clearer. We explain the
origin and formation of the magmatic conduits identified by drawing comparisons to long-distance
lateral magma transport mechanisms observed on Earth. Pressure gradients caused by the
prolonged and extensive volcanic activity in the Marius Hills region compared to the plumbing
system beneath the PKTborder (Lines 347-361) and horizontal pressure gradients along the PKT
rift (Lines 362-371) can account for the origin and formation process. Moreover, fragmented Lunar
Megaregolith (Lines 340-346), reactivation of pre-existing fractures (Lines 357-361), impact-
induced fractures (Lines 373-378), and high heat flow (Lines 390-392) also contribute to this
process. The magmatic conduits between the PKT border structures and the Marius Hills intrusions
account for the compositional distinction between the domes and surrounding and embaying mare
in the Marius region, which might also contribute to the floor-filling process in the Marius crater
(Lines 393-415), highlighting the role of the magmatic conduits in their impact on the volcanic
evolution in the Procellarum Oceanus region.
We expanded the discussion to cover the broader implications of our findings in the Oceanus
Procellarum region (see Lines 440-446) and updated the abstract to reflect these changes. We
particularly highlight the critical role of lateral magma transport in the Moon's volcanic evolution,
which was not discovered before. Understanding these lateral transport mechanisms is crucial for
advancing our knowledge of lunar volcanic processes and should be an important consideration in
future research efforts.
Comments: [264-265] This discussion of vertical dikes vs lateral sills raises a question - previous
work interpreted the linear structures as related to dike-like structures based on their linearity. In
the new interpretation in this study, why are the elongated gravity anomalies that connect the MH
anomalies to each other and to the PKT border structures linear? The gravity inversions are
consistent with sill-like intrusions, but those sill like intrusions are greatly elongated in one
direction.
Response: Thank you for your comments. The magmatic conduits resulting from long-distance
lateral transport on Earth commonly exhibit linear characteristics; please refer to the literature (e.g.,
Gudmundsson et al., 2016; Ishizuka et al., 2017; Sigmundsson et al., 2015; Wilding et al., 2023).
Regarding the linearity exhibited by the magmatic conduits connecting the Marius-SH, Marius-
NH intrusions, and PKT border structures, as we explained in the Discussion, this is mainly
associated with the gradient pressure and impact-induced fractures. The prolonged and extensive
volcanic activity in the Marius Hills region could have caused pressure gradients between the
plumbing system beneath the PKT border and the Marius Hills region. These pressure gradients
could have facilitated rapid magma propagation through the fractures from the PKT border to the
Marius-SH and Marius-NH areas, resulting in linear magmatic conduit structures between these
volcanic systems. Moreover, the magmatic conduit connecting Marius-SH and Marius-NH shows
a NNW–SSE trend that aligns with the regional trend in the Marius Hills region, which is
considered to be related to pre-existing weak zones/fractures (Arya et al., 2018; Raitala, 1980).
Please refer to the Discussion for details.

and southern halves of the Marius Hills was proposed by Kiefer (2013). This research, for the first
time, provides evidence for the connected subsurface structures not only for the MHVC but also
for the adjacent regions.
Further, this finding of interlinked subsurface magmatic structures is also suggested to be
accountable for the existing ages and compositional differences between the older domes of the
MHVC and the younger mare flows in the region. This paper proposes that the younger mare flows
of the MHVC could have been originated from the deep feeder dykes beneath the western border
of the Procellarum terrain as these regions exhibit a connected subsurface magmatic structure in
the derived 3D density models.
Two previously undiscovered magmatic intrusions situated west of the northern Marius intrusion
and to the southwest of the Reiner crater have also been detected for the very first time from the
derived density models of this paper. These newly identified magmatic bodies are inferred to serve
as potential filled and buried impact craters.

magma plumbing system and their subsurface behaviour as the norm. It highlights the importance
of looking at the regional geological context while examining magmatism in a region on the Moon.
However, the arguments presented in the study needs to be substantiated by the compositional and
temporal relationships to build a complete picture of volcanism in the Oceanus Procellarum. In

incorporated within the manuscript:

Marius Hills volcanic complex and the Aristarchus plateau. The results reveal a number of density anomalies consistent with
large intrusions, consistent with previous studies. The results also reveal an interconnection of these density anomalies and
connection to the nearby border structures surrounding the Procellarum region. These results suggest an interconnected
magmatic system responsible for both the border anomalies and prominent volcanic regions.
Overall, I find the authors have satisfactorily replied to my previous comments and revised the manuscript accordingly. The
results of this study are noteworthy and will be of interest to many in the planetary science community. The manuscript is
well written, the analyses are robust, and the conclusions are well supported. Below I have a number of minor comments for
consideration by the authors.
